bibl.title: Response priming driven by local contrast, not subjective brightness

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: Indeed, the experiment clearly shows that priming effects reverse in exactly those conditions in which the flankers’ local contrast to the background reverses, indicating that it is, indeed, local flanker-to-background contrast that drove the priming effect.

span.label: response priming by luminance flankers
span.quote: Response priming by luminance flankers depends neither on the actual physical luminances of the flankers nor on their subjective brightness, as assessed in a psychophysical matching task; instead, it seems to depend exclusively on the local luminance contrast of the flankers to their immediate background.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: They were instructed to keep their eyes on the fixation point and to respond as quickly and correctly as possible, pressing the key on the side where the brighter target was presented.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The feedforward sweeps triggered in turn by flankers and targets still carry only local contrast information, so motor activation is driven by raw local contrast while conscious brightness is settled later by recurrent interactions.
span.quote: this view suggests that the feedforward sweeps successively triggered by the flankers and targets are still dominated by local contrast signals.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Conscious lightness and brightness are computed later, by recurrent processing that trails the initial feedforward wave.
span.quote: The conscious perception of lightness and brightness will be determined later in processing, probably as the result of recurrent interactions trailing behind the initial processing wave

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Response priming accesses a stimulus representation that precedes lightness constancy, i.e. one that has not yet discounted illumination.
span.quote: We adopt the less radical view that response priming reflects a stimulus representation that is earlier and less elaborate than the one underlying conscious vision and, consequently, deficient in lightness constancy.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Placing the high-luminance flanker on the lighted segment turns it into a local decrement (and the low-luminance flanker on the shadowed segment into a local increment), which is what inverts the priming sign.
span.quote: In the attenuation condition, however, the high-luminance flanker was a local decrement because it appeared on an even more luminant background

span.label: Experiments 1 and 2 leave open the alternative that participants judged targets by local contrast sign rather than brightness (addressed only by Experiment 3).
span.quote: However, a possibility remains that the participants never responded to the brightness of the targets in the first place.

span.label: The dissociation licenses only the weaker conclusion that some aspects of lightness constancy are missing from response activation, not that constancy is wholly absent.
span.quote: If priming effects are in systematic disagreement with the flankers’ perceived brightness values, this suggests that at least some aspects of lightness constancy are absent from the response activation process.

span.label: response priming
span.quote: Response priming by luminance flankers depends neither on the actual physical luminances of the flankers nor on their subjective brightness, as assessed in a psychophysical matching task; instead, it seems to depend exclusively on the local luminance contrast of the flankers to their immediate background

span.label: subjective brightness
span.quote: Response priming by luminance flankers depends neither on the actual physical luminances of the flankers nor on their subjective brightness, as assessed in a psychophysical matching task; instead, it seems to depend exclusively on the local luminance contrast of the flankers to their immediate background

span.label: local luminance contrast
span.quote: Response priming by luminance flankers depends neither on the actual physical luminances of the flankers nor on their subjective brightness, as assessed in a psychophysical matching task; instead, it seems to depend exclusively on the local luminance contrast of the flankers to their immediate background

span.label: lightness constancy
span.quote: If priming effects are in systematic disagreement with the flankers’ perceived brightness values, this suggests that at least some aspects of lightness constancy are absent from the response activation process

span.label: **A QUALITATIVE DISSOCIATION, AND IT IS A REVERSAL RATHER THAN AN ATTENUATION:** `These findings indicate a QUALITATIVE DISSOCIATION between the subjective brightness of the stimuli and their propensity for priming a motor response: EVEN THOUGH ONE STIMULUS CAN APPEAR BRIGHTER THAN ANOTHER, IT CAN TRIGGER RESPONSES AS IF IT WERE DARKER.` Not a smaller effect in one condition - **the sign flips**, while the observer's own brightness match goes the other way. A quantitative dissociation can be argued about with a power analysis; a reversal cannot
span.quote: These findings indicate a qualitative dissociation between the subjective brightness of the stimuli and their propensity for priming a motor response: Even though one stimulus can appear brighter than another, it can trigger responses as if it were darker

span.label: **AND THE CONTROL THAT MAKES THIS DIFFERENT IN KIND FROM EVERY OTHER DISSOCIATION IN THIS CORPUS:** `Note that this dissociation MAKES NO USE OF VISUAL MASKING OR BRIEF STIMULUS PRESENTATIONS OF ANY KIND: It is obtained even though the presented stimuli are ALL IN PLAIN VIEW, and it relies solely on characteristic differences in processing dynamics between the priming and matching tasks.` **dehaene1998 flashes a numeral for 43 ms between masks; marcel1983, holcomb2005 and Finkbeiner2011 all argue about whether the prime was seen. This paper lets the observer look straight at it.** So the gap is not between seen and unseen but between two live representations of one visible stimulus - which is a different claim, needing none of the machinery the awareness literature spends its credibility on
span.quote: Note that this dissociation makes no use of visual masking or brief stimulus presentations of any kind: It is obtained even though the presented stimuli are all in plain view, and it relies solely on characteristic differences in processing dynamics

span.label: **THE CLAIM IS A TRIPLE NEGATIVE THAT NAMES ITS WINNER:** `Response priming by luminance flankers depends NEITHER on the actual physical luminances of the flankers NOR on their subjective brightness, as assessed in a psychophysical matching task; instead, it seems to depend EXCLUSIVELY on the LOCAL LUMINANCE CONTRAST of the flankers to their immediate background.` **The two excluded candidates are the physical variable and the perceptual variable** - between them, everything anyone would have guessed - and each was excluded by a measurement rather than by an argument. The third is named, and it is a property of the stimulus's relation to its own neighbourhood
span.quote: Response priming by luminance flankers depends neither on the actual physical luminances of the flankers nor on their subjective brightness, as assessed in a psychophysical matching task; instead, it seems to depend exclusively on the local luminance contrast of the flankers to their immediate background

span.label: **AND THE INFERENCE IS CAREFULLY PARTIAL:** `If priming effects are in systematic disagreement with the flankers' perceived brightness values, this suggests that AT LEAST SOME ASPECTS of lightness constancy are ABSENT FROM THE RESPONSE ACTIVATION PROCESS.` **`at least some aspects` and `suggests` are both in the quote**, and they are the difference between this and a claim that the motor pathway is pre-constancy. The illusion used here IS a consequence of lightness constancy - the authors say so - so its failure to reach the response is evidence about one pathway, not a map of the visual system
span.quote: If priming effects are in systematic disagreement with the flankers’ perceived brightness values, this suggests that at least some aspects of lightness constancy are absent from the response activation process

span.label: builds-on → Moore and Brown (2001), visual search under a dark transparent filter
span.quote: Our conclusions are in agreement with a study by Moore and Brown (2001), in which visual search for highluminance and low-luminance targets was performed under conditions in which parts of the display seemed to be watched through a dark transparent filter.

span.label: contradicts → physiological studies reporting that subjective lightness is signalled early in the hierarchy (MacEvoy & Paradiso, 2001; Rossi & Paradiso, 1999; Rossi, Rittenhouse, & Paradiso, 1996)
span.quote: This conclusion might seem to conflict with some physiological studies showing that subjective lightness is signaled early in the processing hierarchy, such that the responses of many cells in the primary visual cortex (V1) and even some in the lateral geniculate nucleus are modulated by a simultaneous contrast illusion (MacEvoy & Par-rr adiso, 2001; Rossi & Paradiso, 1999; Rossi, Rittenhouse, & Paradiso, 1996).

span.label: contradicts → Breitmeyer, Ro, and Singhal (2004), the proposal that response priming is based on raw physical stimulus characteristics rather than perceived color; the authors explicitly adopt a "less radical view" in the next sentence
span.quote: Breitmeyer, Ro, and Singhal (2004; Breitmeyer, Ö(cid:120)(cid:129) men, & Chen, 2004) have proposed that response priming is based on raw physical stimulus characteristics, such as the distribution of wavelength information, instead of perceived color. We adopt the less radical view that response priming reflects a stimulus representation that is earlier and less elaborate than the one underlying conscious vision and, consequently, deficient in lightness constancy

span.label: builds-on → the rapid-chase model of response priming (Schmidt et al., 2006; Schmidt & Schmidt, 2009)
span.quote: In the framework of the rapid-chase model of response priming (Schmidt et al., 2006; Schmidt & Schmidt, 2009), this view suggests that the feedforward sweeps successively triggered by the flankers and targets are still dominated by local contrast signals.

span.label: local luminance contrast —causes→ response priming
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.95 — **`EXCLUSIVELY` IS IN THE QUOTE AND IT IS THE WHOLE CLAIM.** Two rival causes are named and excluded in the same sentence - physical luminance and subjective brightness - so this is not `X is associated with Y` but `X and not the two things you would have guessed`. Weight 0.95: the general discussion's opening sentence, resting on a systematic variation of the illusion rather than on one contrast. `increases` means more local contrast in the priming direction yields more priming, and the reversal condition is the same relation with the contrast sign flipped.
span.quote: Response priming by luminance flankers depends neither on the actual physical luminances of the flankers nor on their subjective brightness, as assessed in a psychophysical matching task; instead, it seems to depend exclusively on the local luminance contrast of the flankers to their immediate background

span.label: response priming —distinct-from→ subjective brightness
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — **A REVERSAL, NOT AN ATTENUATION, AND THAT IS WHY THIS EARNS 0.95.** `distinct-from` usually records that two concepts are not the same thing; here the quote shows them moving in OPPOSITE directions on the same stimulus - one flanker appears brighter and primes as if darker. **And the second sense is what makes it valuable: no masking, no brief presentation, the stimuli in plain view.** Every other dissociation in this corpus separates a seen thing from an unseen thing; this separates two representations of a thing the observer is looking at.
span.quote: Response priming by luminance flankers depends neither on the actual physical luminances of the flankers nor on their subjective brightness, as assessed in a psychophysical matching task; instead, it seems to depend exclusively on the local luminance contrast of the flankers to their immediate background

span.label: repeated-measures ANOVA
span.quote: Repeated measures ANOVAs were performed with Greenhouse–Geisser-corrected p values.

span.label: Greenhouse-Geisser correction
span.quote: Repeated measures ANOVAs were performed with Greenhouse–Geisser-corrected p values.

span.label: arcsine transformation
span.quote: Error rates were arcsine transformed to match ANOVA requirements.

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: Error bars represent standard errors of the means corrected for intersubject variance (Bakeman & McArthur, 1996; cf. Loftus & Masson, 1994).

span.label: When the illusion made the two flankers look similar in brightness, the priming effect reversed sign: consistent flankers slowed responses and inconsistent flankers speeded them.
span.quote: But when the illumination attenuates perceived flanker differences, priming effects unexpectedly are reversed: Responses become slower with consistent flankers and faster with inconsistent flankers.

span.label: The same flanker could look brighter than its partner while priming the response assigned to the darker stimulus.
span.quote: In other words, in the attenuation condition, the more luminant flanker looks brighter than the other flanker but primes as if it were darker.

span.label: Brightness matching never reversed: the physically more luminant flanker was always judged the brighter one in every illusion condition.
span.quote: As in the previous experiments, the matching task revealed that the physically more luminant flanker was always judged brighter than the less luminant one in all the illusion conditions.

span.label: Varying the light-to-shadow ratio showed that priming flipped sign in exactly the conditions where each flanker's contrast against its own background flipped from increment to decrement.
span.quote: Indeed, the experiment clearly shows that priming effects reverse in exactly those conditions in which the flankers’ local contrast to the background reverses, indicating that it is, indeed, local flanker-to-background contrast that drove the priming effect.

span.label: The reversal survived when targets were made all-decrement or all-increment pairs, so participants could not have been responding to target contrast sign alone.
span.quote: Despite these changes, Experiment 3 replicated the finding that priming effects are strongly positive in enhancement conditions but are reversed in attenuation conditions, in which the flankers switch their

span.label: Overall, response priming tracked neither the flankers' physical luminance nor their perceived brightness, but only their local luminance contrast against the immediately surrounding background.
span.quote: Response priming by luminance flankers depends neither on the actual physical luminances of the flankers nor on their subjective brightness, as assessed in a psychophysical matching task; instead, it seems to depend exclusively on the local luminance contrast of the flankers to their immediate background.

span.label: The priming-perception dissociation was obtained with all stimuli fully visible, without masking or brief presentation.
span.quote: Note that this dissociation makes no use of visual masking or brief stimulus presentations of any kind: It is obtained even though the presented stimuli are all in plain view

span.label: lightness versus brightness
span.quote: The term lightness is defined as the subjectively perceived reflectance of a surface, whereas the term brightness refers to its perceived luminance.

span.label: lightness constancy
span.quote: This system’s most basic task is to achieve lightness constancy by telling differences in reflectance (the percentage of light a surface reflects into the observer’s eye) from differences in illumination (the amount of light incident on that surface

span.label: rapid-chase theory of response priming
span.quote: The rapid-chase theory of response priming (Schmidt et al., 2006; Schmidt & Schmidt, 2009) therefore proposes that response priming is based on sequential, nonoverlapping waves of rapid feedforward activation

span.label: priming effect (operational definition)
span.quote: Priming effects were defined as RT differences in the consistent and inconsistent conditions

span.label: flanker-target consistency
span.quote: On consistent trials, each flanker had the same luminance as its adjacent target, whereas on inconsistent trials, flanker luminances were spatially switched with respect to target luminances.

span.label: response time to the target
span.quote: RT was defined as the time interval from target onset to registered keypress.

span.label: matched luminance in the brightness-matching task
span.term: matched luminance in the brightness-matching task
span.quote: In a separate brightness-matching session, the participants used the computer keyboard to freely adjust the luminances of the targets to match the perceived luminance of the flankers.

span.label: physical luminance of the flankers
span.quote: Even though the flankers always had the same two luminance levels as the targets, their perceived brightness values depended on their placement on the different segments of the folded plane

span.label: Eight — participants in Experiment 1
span.quote: Eight students from the University of Giessen (19–24 years of age, all female, 1 left-handed, all with normal or corrected-to-normal vision) participated for payment or course credit after giving informed consent.

span.label: 1.0, 34.2, and 11.1 cd/m2 — luminances of the shadowed, lighted and neutrally illuminated segments of the folded plane in Experiment 1
span.quote: the shadowed, lighted, and neutrally illuminated (frontoparallel) segments had luminances of 1.0, 34.2, and 11.1 cd/m2, respectively.

span.label: 17, 33, 50, 67, or 83 msec — the flanker-target SOAs used in Experiment 1
span.quote: Following a flanker– target SOA of 17, 33, 50, 67, or 83 msec, the two targets appeared to the left and right of the fixation point on the midsegment 1,500 msec after the onset of the plane.

span.label: 0.19% — share of Experiment 1 trials discarded as RT outliers
span.quote: RTs shorter than 100 msec or longer than 800 msec were discarded as outliers (0.19% of the data).

span.quote: Overall, RTs were about 30 msec shorter for mixed targets than for decrement or increment targets
